title: Late Payment Reminder Emails: 5 Templates That Get You Paid
description: Five copy-paste late payment reminder email templates, from a friendly nudge to a final notice, plus subject lines, timing, and tips to get paid faster.
html:
Most late invoices are not a sign of a bad client. They are usually stuck in an inbox, waiting on an approval, or missing a detail. A clear, well-timed reminder solves most of them. Below are five templates that escalate gradually, from a friendly heads-up to a final notice. Replace the bracketed parts, keep the tone, and send.

Before you send any reminder

Check these three things first. They are the most common reasons an invoice goes unpaid, and fixing them is faster than chasing.

  • Was the invoice received by the right person? If you sent it to your project contact, it may never have reached accounts payable.
  • Does it include everything the client needs? PO number, correct company name, and clear payment details.
  • Is the due date unambiguous? An actual date such as 26 October is harder to miss than Net 14.

If you are not confident in the invoice itself, regenerate a clean copy with our free invoice maker and attach it to your reminder.

A suggested reminder schedule

There is no single correct schedule, but this one works well for most freelancers and small businesses:

WhenTemplateTone
3 days before due date1. Friendly pre-reminderHelpful
1 day after due date2. Gentle overdue nudgePolite
7 days overdue3. Firm follow-upDirect
14 to 21 days overdue4. EscalationSerious
30+ days overdue5. Final noticeFormal

Adjust the timing to your payment terms and relationship. A long-standing client who always pays eventually might warrant a phone call at stage 3 instead of an email.

Template 1: Friendly pre-reminder (before the due date)

This is not a chase. It simply puts your invoice back at the top of the inbox before it is late.

Subject: Invoice [number] due on [date]

Hi [Name],

Just a quick heads-up that invoice [number] for [project/service], totalling [amount], is due on [date]. I've attached a copy for convenience.

Payment details are on the invoice. Let me know if you need anything from me to get it processed.

Thanks,

[Your name]

Template 2: Gentle overdue nudge (1 day late)

Assume good faith. Most invoices at this stage were simply missed.

Subject: Quick reminder: invoice [number] was due yesterday

Hi [Name],

I hope all is well. I wanted to check in on invoice [number] for [amount], which was due on [date]. I haven't seen the payment come through yet, so I've reattached the invoice in case it got lost.

If it's already been paid, please ignore this and thank you. If there's anything holding it up, just let me know and I'll sort it out.

Best,

[Your name]

Template 3: Firm follow-up (7 days late)

Now be more direct and ask a specific question. Questions get answers; statements get ignored.

Subject: Invoice [number] is now 7 days overdue

Hi [Name],

Invoice [number] for [amount] was due on [date] and is now 7 days overdue. Could you let me know when I can expect payment?

If the invoice needs to go to someone else for approval, please share their contact details and I'll follow up directly. I've attached the invoice again for reference.

Thanks,

[Your name]

Template 4: Escalation (14 to 21 days late)

At this point, copy in a second contact, such as accounts payable or the person who hired you. Mention any consequences you agreed in your contract, such as pausing work or late fees.

Subject: Overdue payment: invoice [number] ([amount]) - action needed

Hi [Name],

I'm following up again on invoice [number] for [amount], which was due on [date] and is now [X] days overdue. I haven't yet received a payment date despite my previous reminders on [dates].

As outlined in our agreement, I'll need to pause further work on [project] until this invoice is settled. Per our terms, a late fee of [amount or %] may also apply from [date].

Please confirm a payment date by [date, e.g. 3 business days from now]. I'd much prefer to resolve this quickly and keep working together.

Regards,

[Your name]

Only mention late fees or interest if they were in your contract or invoice terms, or are allowed by law where you operate. Rules differ between countries and states, so check local rules before applying charges.

Template 5: Final notice (30+ days late)

This is the last email before you take further action. Keep it calm, factual, and specific about what happens next and when.

Subject: Final notice: invoice [number] - [amount] overdue since [date]

Dear [Name],

This is a final notice regarding invoice [number] for [amount], which was due on [date] and remains unpaid after reminders sent on [dates].

Please arrange full payment by [date, e.g. 7 days from now]. If payment is not received by then, I will [refer the debt to a collection agency / begin small claims proceedings / apply statutory interest and compensation], without further notice.

If there is a problem with the invoice or you would like to agree a payment plan, please reply before that date and I will be glad to discuss it.

Sincerely,

[Your name]

Do not threaten an action you are not prepared to take. If you are considering legal action, small claims court or a formal letter before action may be the next step, but the process varies by jurisdiction. Check local rules or get advice first.

Subject lines that get opened

The subject line matters more than the body. Include the invoice number and something concrete. Some alternatives:

  • Invoice [number] - payment due [date]
  • Following up: invoice [number] for [project]
  • Can you confirm a payment date for invoice [number]?
  • Invoice [number] now [X] days overdue

Avoid vague subjects like Just checking in. They are easy to skip and do not tell the reader what you need.

Tips that make reminders work

  • Always attach the invoice. Never make the client search for it.
  • Reply in the same thread. It shows the history of your reminders at a glance.
  • Ask a question. When can I expect payment? is harder to ignore than a statement.
  • Make paying easy. Include a payment link or bank details in the email body, not just the attachment.
  • Stay professional. Your emails may be read by people you have never met, and may matter later if there is a dispute.
  • Keep records. Note when each reminder was sent. You may need this if you escalate.
  • Pick up the phone. After two unanswered emails, a short call often resolves things faster.

About late fees and interest

Some places give businesses a legal right to charge interest on late commercial payments. In the UK, for example, the Late Payment of Commercial Debts (Interest) Act lets businesses claim statutory interest and fixed compensation on overdue business-to-business invoices. Other countries, states, and provinces have different rules, and some only allow late fees that were agreed in advance. Check local rules, and state any late fee clearly in your contract and on your invoice.

Prevent the next late payment

The best reminder is the one you never have to send. Set clear payment terms before work starts, invoice promptly, show the due date as a real date, and make payment details hard to miss.
